bubbles.text: The fires in camp went cold sometime in the night. No one came to wake me.
I think that means it has begun.
Father said: dress, eat, ride. In that order. Don't think about the third thing until you've done the first two.
I will pretend I am still sleeping for a moment longer.
He covered the embers before he left. He always did. As if a tidy hearth could bring him back to it.
He rode out three nights ago with Sultan Batyr's vanguard. I have not seen him since. I do not allow myself to count the nights.
Mother's tumar. She made me promise to wear it the first time I rode to a fight.
I have been postponing today for two years.

[Folded inside the tumar - a strip of birch bark, in mother's hand:]
Aitugan - for the day you are afraid. Wear it. Then take it off. The Aruakh do not protect the timid.
Hm. Thank you, mother.
String it. Test it. Don't pluck the cord like an idiot in front of the older girls. Father's three rules of archery.
He never had a fourth. I have suspected, lately, that there should be a fourth.
Sharp. Light. Decent for skinning a hare. We will see what else.
Not yet. I am not finished here.
Every yurt empty. Every fire dead. Six hundred of us, they say. They left without me.
...horns... the eastern slope... matchlocks to the trench...
The pass is half a day's ride. Less, if I am honest with the horse.
Burken. You and I. Try not to throw me into a ravine before I have at least drawn the bow.
Six hundred of us. They say there are fifty thousand of them. I do not believe in numbers anymore.
Six paces deep. They were not exaggerating.
The slot to my left is empty. The man who was supposed to stand there is not here. I do not ask why.
...hold the line... matchlocks loaded... the Khan says wait for the horn...
A bow, a fire, a wall of dirt. Three friends today.

[Stained order, in formal script:]
By order of Jangir, Sultan Batyr: each archer shall hold their slot. None shall break ranks for a wounded comrade until the horn sounds twice. The pass narrows at the throat. They cannot bring their full number to bear if we hold.
...incoming... eastern slope... loose...
Shoot. Nock. Shoot. Nock. There is no other thought.
...the trench at the throat is holding... the right flank, where is the right flank...
I can hear the matchlocks. Three of them, somewhere up the line. They are louder than I expected. They smell worse than I expected.

[Scrap of paper, folded small, half-burnt:]
...Jangir has ordered the trenches dug six paces deep. The pass is narrow. They cannot bring their full number to bear. We need only hold until the Bukharan comes. Yalantos rides hard from Samarkand -
...shields... shields on the second wave... aim the eyes...
The shield. Of course. The fire, then. I am slow today.
There. The fire. Father would have shouted at me for taking that long.
Twenty arrows left. I came with thirty-five. I will not say this number out loud.
...the sun is barely up... we have done one hour of this... one hour...
...matchlock! left side! down he goes -
Whoever shot that, I love you. I do not know your name and I love you.
I have not eaten today. I will not eat today. The saumal will be enough.
...where is the relief... the Bukharan... where...
I think the others are afraid too. It is good to know. It is also not good to know.
...the whole eastern slope... loose, loose, loose!
The girl three slots down. I never asked her name. I will not ask now.
...runner!... we need a runner up the pass... powder!... who'll go!...
I am the smallest one in this trench. I am also the one with breath left. So.
From the trench it sounded big. From up here it sounds small. The wrong way around.
I will count. I will not. I will not count.
(Dzungar speech, from offscreen.)
Two of them. They flanked the pass somehow. Someone will need to know about that, after.
Quiet. Quiet, Aitugan. The wind is loud enough for both of us.

[A travel-prayer, scratched into the rock by some long-ago shepherd:]
Tengri, who walks the high places: let the one who reads this come down again. - Adai, son of Sengir.
He is not one of ours. The robe is too fine. The horse is missing.
A messenger, then. Someone got to him before us.

[A letter in Persian script, half-completed, ink smeared:]
...to Sultan Batyr, from Yalantos Bahadur of Bukhara: My lord, our column is delayed. The Syr crossing flooded two nights past. We will reach Orbulak in two days, not one. Hold. We are coming. Hold. - Y.
Two days.
Two days, not one.
Whoever takes this back to the Khan will be the one who delivers him this number. Not me. Not me, please.
Heavier than it should be. Nine matchlocks left in the trench, perhaps. This will keep them speaking.
(Dzungar voices again, closer this time. A hoof scraping rock.)
I am one nineteen-year-old with a satchel of black powder. If I sneeze, I am a small explosion.
...about time, girl... give it here... the horn... two days you say?... two days...
I did not say it. I gave them the letter. They will say it for me.
Stay low, Aitugan. I'm three paces back. I'm with you.
Whoever you are, walk softer. Your boots are louder than my heart, and that is saying something.
He's asleep. Your call. The Khan said no quarter. The Khan is not in this ravine.
I am not a butcher tonight. I am a girl with seven arrows. He will sleep, and I will walk, and tomorrow neither of us will remember.
Quick. He did not wake. That is the only mercy I owed him.
Father's pack. He came through here. This means he was alive two nights ago.
He is alive somewhere in this dark, then. Or he was.

[A note in his hand, hurriedly written:]
Aitugan - if you find this and not me, take the wind-fletched ones. I never showed you. They do not strike to kill. They strike to push. Sometimes that is the better thing. - B.
He never showed me because I was never patient enough to learn anything that did not strike to kill.
I am sorry, father. I am learning tonight.
Two of them. Left one's mine. Yours is the right. On three.
On three. On three. On -
Down! He's down! Move, mo-
The fragment did not finish.
Maybe they are tying their boot. Maybe they are catching breath.
I will not call out. If they answer, the ravine will know I am alone.
Wind arrow. Now. Now. Now.
I have his blood on my hand and mine on my shoulder. That is not the trade I would have chosen.
The Aruakh watch over me tonight. Also: nobody else does.
Stars. There are still stars. The Dzungars and I share that, at least.
...the high ridge... the signal fire... it must be lit... the Bukharans need the marker... it must be lit...
It must be lit. By whom, the wind did not specify.
The shoulder is stiff. The legs work. The bow is light enough.
Halfway. I will lie to myself: halfway.

[A prayer rag, old, the writing nearly gone:]
...the high places are nearer to Tengri. Walk slow. Breathe.
Someone else is coming up the other path. Their stride is wrong for one of ours.
Of course. Of course they would send someone too. The Bukharan banner would be a problem for them as well.
(He speaks. Dzungar. She does not understand the words. She understands the shape of them.)
I do not know your name. I think you do not know mine. Good.
Mother. I see what you meant.
The flint is colder than I expected. My hands are warmer than I expected. The beacon is taller than I expected.
So they came after all.
Two days and one. Yalantos Bahadur. I will remember the name. He will not remember mine, and that is fair.
I am going to sit down now.
The Battle of Orbulak ended on the third day.
Jangir Khan held the pass. The Dzungars retreated.
Six hundred against fifty thousand, and the steppe remembered.
Aitugan's name is not in any chronicle.
There were many like her.
The Khan summons every batyr's child to Turkistan. He says the Dzungars will return. He says we must be ready.
I am tired. But I will go.
To be continued in Steppe Chronicles, Episode 2.
